analysis.one_liner: Requires nutrition labels on all packaged foods and sets one national labeling standard, overriding state rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it drew no cosponsors and no hearings or vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every packaged food to carry a label listing its protein, carbohydrate, calorie, fat, vitamin, and mineral content, and would have set uniform federal rules for claims like 'high,' 'light,' or 'organic.' It also would have stopped states and cities from writing their own food-labeling rules, except with federal approval, and created an advisory committee of consumers, scientists, and food-industry representatives to guide the Secretary of Health and Human Services. The bill was introduced by Senator Orrin Hatch, referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers buying packaged groceries, who would get standardized nutrition facts on labels nationwide for the first time and uniform definitions for health claims like 'light' or 'organic.' Food manufacturers would also gain a single national standard instead of a patchwork of state rules, and states could still petition to have their rules adopted federally.

how_it_helps.text: Packaged foods could not be sold unless their labels list protein, carbohydrate, calorie, and fat content plus vitamin, mineral, and other dietary properties as the Secretary of Health and Human Services prescribes [S2][S3].

Labels bearing claims like 'high,' 'light,' or 'organic,' or statements relating food to a disease, would be deemed misbranded unless they conform to federal regulations, so shoppers would not have to guess what marketing terms mean [S2][S3].
The bill directs the Secretary to run a nationwide consumer education program about diet, nutrition, and how to read food labels, funded at $5 million per year from 1990 through 1992 [S2][S3].
Food makers would get one national labeling rule instead of differing state and local requirements, which the bill's findings say interfere with federal regulation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Packaged-food manufacturers, who would bear the cost of printing new labels and reformulating claims to meet the rules within the bill's deadlines (labeling regulations within two years, claim rules within one). State and local governments would lose the power to set their own, stricter food-labeling requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local food-labeling laws: no state could keep or create a labeling requirement unless it is identical to the federal rule or wins an exemption for compelling local conditions, and the definition covers any dissemination of food information, including posters and advertising [S2][S3].

The advisory committee that guides the rules must include representatives of the food industry alongside consumer and scientific members, giving regulated companies a formal seat in shaping the standards [S3].

Broad discretion rests with the Secretary: what counts as an acceptable claim, which foods are 'not a meaningful source of nutrients,' and whether exemptions apply would all be decided by regulation rather than by the statute itself [S3].

Small food producers would face the same labeling deadlines as large ones, and fresh produce and restaurant food are entirely exempt, so the most perishable and least-processed foods would remain unlabeled [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Mandatory nutrition labeling is a real, lasting gain for shoppers and is widely credited with improving diets, so the consumer benefit is large. The cost side is real too: preemption trades away states' ability to go further than Washington, and industry sits on the advisory body shaping the rules. On balance the bill helps ordinary people more than it hurts them, but its uniformity bargain favors national food manufacturers as much as consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and Congress ended in January 1991 with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on August 3, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S5].
That referral was the bill's last action; the committee took it up no further, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged-food manufacturers avoided mandatory nutrition-labeling costs and outside state rules for another year, and no one else gained from the bill's death; shoppers waited until the Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990 for mandatory labels.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so support or opposition by party cannot be measured from the record; the sponsor was a senior Republican.

industries.note: The bill imposes mandatory nutrition labeling and regulated health claims, a real cost, but grants the industry's top ask: one national standard that overrides differing state rules. Its interest in the preemption runs against shoppers in states that might have set stricter labels.
States lose authority over food labeling and even local information campaigns like posters and notices, keeping them from setting rules stricter than the federal ceiling.
Terms like 'organic' could no longer be used freely; only Secretary-approved definitions would be allowed. That constrains marketers but protects honest producers against loose claims.
They are expressly exempt from labeling requirements, avoiding any compliance cost while providing no nutrition information at the point of sale.
